transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, nice to meet you. Um, well, I guess what brings me in is that I’m just... exhausted. But it's in a way that sleep doesn’t really fix at all. Like, even just getting through a normal workday at the office—I'm a manager, so there's always something going on—and then coming home to make dinner just feels so much heavier than it should. 

Actually, speaking of dinner, I tried making this new chicken bake thing last night because my sister keeps sending me these meal prep reels on Instagram. She lives out in Arizona now, which is gorgeous, but honestly, the heat there is just unbelievable in the summer. I don't know how she stands it, especially with her two golden retrievers. They shed everywhere, and I told her she needs to get one of those robot vacuums, you know? I bought one on sale last Black Friday and it's been okay, but it always gets stuck under the sofa. 

But um... yeah, anyway, I'm just here because getting through the day and making a simple meal just feels really, really heavy lately.
How long have you been feeling this exhausted and weighed down—days, weeks, or longer?

Well, it's been going on for about a month now. Which is strange, because right before this, I was actually feeling really... driven, I guess? Like, I had all this energy at work and was getting so much done. I reorganized the entire filing system for my department, which honestly was a disaster. The previous manager, Tom, he just shoved everything into these manila folders without labeling them properly. I don't understand how people can work like that, you know? It's like my neighbor, Susan, she leaves her recycling bins out on the curb for three days after pickup. It drives the HOA crazy. They send out these passive-aggressive newsletters every month, printed on this really cheap yellow paper. 

But um, yeah, before this last month of feeling so low and heavy, I was actually doing really well and had a ton of energy. Now I just can't seem to find that again.
During that month or so when you felt unusually driven and energetic, about how many days in a row did that elevated energy last?

Um, it was probably for a couple of weeks, straight. I just had so much energy during that time. I was bouncing between all these work projects, taking calls for the art committee, and coming up with all these home organization ideas... it was like I just couldn’t slow down. 

Actually, speaking of the art committee, we were trying to put together the spring silent auction, and you would not believe how hard it is to get local businesses to donate gift baskets lately. I mean, the bakery downtown—the one with the amazing sourdough, I always get a loaf on Sundays because it's just perfectly crusty—they wouldn't even return my emails. And I know the owner, Greg! His daughter actually goes to college with my niece up in Oregon. My niece is studying marine biology, which sounds fascinating, but she has to do all these freezing early morning boat trips out on the water, and I just don't know how she handles the cold. I hate being cold. I have to wear fuzzy socks around the house starting in October. 

But um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, yeah, the energy lasted for a couple of weeks.

During those two weeks of high energy, did it cause any serious problems—like conflicts at work, risky decisions, or needing hospitalization—or were you still able to function normally aside from feeling unusually driven?

No, no, nothing like that. I didn't need a hospital or anything, and I wasn't getting into arguments. If anything, I was functioning better than normal. I was getting to the office so early I actually got a parking spot in the front lot for once. Usually, if you get there past 8:15, you have to park way out by the old strip mall. 

And that lot is just covered in seagulls, which makes no sense because we are at least an hour from the beach. They made an absolute mess of my windshield a while back. I had to go to the drive-thru car wash on my lunch break, the one with the big spinning blue brushes? I always get a little claustrophobic in those things, to be honest. It feels like you're trapped in a soapy tunnel. My friend Brenda loves them, though. She gets the premium wax every single time she goes, which I think is a waste of money, but she insists it protects the paint. She drives this bright red convertible, so I guess she cares more about that stuff than I do. 

But um... wait, yeah, no serious problems. I was just really productive and getting a lot done.
During that two-week period of high energy, did anyone in your life—like coworkers, family, or friends—comment that you seemed unusually different from your normal self?

I don't think so... I mean, nobody really said anything to me about it. My sister called me a lot around then, but she usually just calls to vent about her dog. She has this Goldendoodle, Bailey, and he has the most incredibly sensitive stomach. She actually has to boil organic chicken and brown rice for him every single night. I told her she's spoiling him, but she treats that dog like an actual baby. 

Which is funny, because her actual baby—my nephew, Tyler—just started middle school, and she was complaining about his school supply list. They make them buy these incredibly specific graphing calculators now. Do you remember when just a basic calculator was fine? Now it's like a hundred and twenty dollars for a calculator that he's probably going to lose on the bus anyway. Kids lose everything. I used to lose my umbrellas all the time when I was his age, I'd just leave them on the seat of the train. 

But um, what were we talking about? Oh, if people noticed I was different. No, I don't think anyone mentioned anything. They were probably just happy I was getting so much work done, honestly.
During those two weeks of high energy, did you notice you needed less sleep than usual but still felt rested?

Yeah, actually, that was one of the weirdest parts. I was only sleeping maybe four hours a night during that stretch, but I'd wake up feeling totally fine. Like, I'd pop out of bed ready to send emails, sketch out event ideas, or reorganize the kitchen cabinets. 

I actually ended up pulling everything out of my pantry one of those mornings because I decided I needed to put all the dry goods in those clear acrylic bins. You know the ones? They look so nice on Pinterest, but honestly, they are so expensive. I went to that container store out by the mall, and I swear I spent a small fortune just on plastic boxes. And the labels! You have to buy a specific label maker if you want it to look uniform. I got this one that connects to your phone via Bluetooth, which is neat, but it took me an hour just to figure out the app. My phone is always running out of storage anyway because I take too many pictures of my garden. My hydrangeas were absolutely out of control this year. I had to cut back so many blooms, and I tried drying them, but they just get so crumbly and make a mess everywhere. 

But um... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, sleep. Yeah, I was getting about four hours and feeling completely rested, ready to go.

During this past month of feeling heavy and exhausted, have you also noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, along with feelings of guilt or worthlessness, or trouble concentrating?

Yeah, it's been really hard to care about much of anything lately. I usually love painting, and I'd spend my weekends wandering through museum exhibits, just soaking it all in. But recently, my paints are just sitting there untouched on the easel. I can't even make myself care enough to go to a museum. 

Which is a shame, because the art museum downtown just opened that new impressionist exhibit. I saw the banners for it when I was driving back from the dentist last week. I really hate going to the dentist, by the way. The hygienist always scolds me about flossing, but I swear my gums are just naturally sensitive. She recommended this specific water flosser, the one with the different pressure settings? I bought it off Amazon, but it takes up so much space on my bathroom counter. I have this tiny pedestal sink, which looks very vintage and charming, but it is completely impractical for actually holding things like soap or toothpaste. I keep telling myself I'm going to remodel that bathroom and put in a proper vanity, maybe something with brushed nickel hardware. I saw some beautiful drawer pulls at the hardware store when I was looking for a new latch for my garden gate. 

But um... wait, I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. Oh, right, the exhaustion. Yeah, I just haven't had the interest to do my painting or anything I usually enjoy. I just feel so drained.

During that two-week period when you had so much energy, did you notice feeling unusually self-confident, like you could do anything or that your ideas were especially brilliant compared to how you normally feel about yourself?

Oh, absolutely. I was honestly convinced I could fix the whole department morale problem at work, and even all our family routines at home, if everyone would just get on board with my plan. I felt like my ideas were completely foolproof. I actually bought these giant whiteboards for the office to map out the new workflow. 

Which, by the way, whiteboards are incredibly hard to transport in a sedan. I had to put the back seats down in my Honda, and even then, the corner kept poking into the back of my headrest. I love that car, though. It has that really nice seat warmer feature, which is an absolute lifesaver in the winter. My husband’s truck doesn't have seat warmers, and the leather gets so freezing cold in January. He’s been talking about trading it in for a hybrid, but the waitlists for the ones he wants are like six months long right now. The dealership actually called him last week about a cancellation, but it was in this awful bright orange color. Who buys a bright orange truck? It looks like a giant traffic cone. You'd never be able to lose it in a parking lot, I guess, which would be nice. I always lose my car at the grocery store. I have to wander around pressing the lock button on my keys just to hear the horn beep. 

But um... wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost track of what we were talking about. Did you ask about the office? No, wait... my confidence, right. Yeah, I just felt really, really capable, like my plans were brilliant and I could fix everything.

doctor.intent: Assess for another core hypomanic symptom (inflated self-esteem/grandiosity) to determine if full DSM-5 criteria for a hypomanic episode are met, which helps differentiate Bipolar II (F31.81) from unspecified bipolar disorder (F31.9)
doctor.question: During that two-week period when you had so much energy, did you notice feeling unusually self-confident, like you could do anything or that your ideas were especially brilliant compared to how you normally feel about yourself?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I was honestly convinced I could fix the whole department morale problem and our family routines if everyone would just get on board with my plan.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I felt unusually self-confident or had brilliant ideas during the high-energy period, which maps to inflated self-esteem.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. I was honestly convinced I could fix the whole department morale problem at work, and even all our family routines at home, if everyone would just get on board with my plan. I felt like my ideas were completely foolproof. I actually bought these giant whiteboards for the office to map out the new workflow. 

Which, by the way, whiteboards are incredibly hard to transport in a sedan. I had to put the back seats down in my Honda, and even then, the corner kept poking into the back of my headrest. I love that car, though. It has that really nice seat warmer feature, which is an absolute lifesaver in the winter. My husband’s truck doesn't have seat warmers, and the leather gets so freezing cold in January. He’s been talking about trading it in for a hybrid, but the waitlists for the ones he wants are like six months long right now. The dealership actually called him last week about a cancellation, but it was in this awful bright orange color. Who buys a bright orange truck? It looks like a giant traffic cone. You'd never be able to lose it in a parking lot, I guess, which would be nice. I always lose my car at the grocery store. I have to wander around pressing the lock button on my keys just to hear the horn beep. 

But um... wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost track of what we were talking about. Did you ask about the office? No, wait... my confidence, right. Yeah, I just felt really, really capable, like my plans were brilliant and I could fix everything.

inference.note: The patient's two-week period of elevated mood featured decreased need for sleep with preserved energy, increased goal-directed activity, inflated self-esteem/grandiosity, and no significant impairment, hospitalization, or psychosis—consistent with a hypomanic (not manic) episode. Combined with the current one-month major depressive episode (anhedonia, fatigue, low mood), this pattern fits Bipolar II Disorder, ruling out unspecified bipolar disorder (F31.9).

opening_question.intent: Establish the primary reason for the visit today
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a discrete ~2-week period of elevated, goal-directed energy with decreased need for sleep (4 hrs, feeling rested), grandiosity/inflated self-confidence, increased goal-directed activity (reorganizing filing system, pantry, whiteboards), and distractibility/tangential speech, without hospitalization, psychosis, or marked functional impairment—consistent with a hypomanic episode rather than mania. This was immediately followed by a ~1-month major depressive episode with pervasive fatigue not relieved by sleep, anhedonia (loss of interest in painting/museums), and functional heaviness in daily tasks. The combination of a hypomanic episode and a major depressive episode, without any history of full manic episode, supports Bipolar II Disorder, current episode depressed.
